technical_table_id <- function(index) {
  if (!is.numeric(index) || length(index) != 1L || !is.finite(index) ||
      index < 1 || index != floor(index))
    stop("Technical table index must be a positive integer.")
  label <- character()
  while (index > 0) {
    label <- c(LETTERS[(index - 1) %% 26 + 1], label)
    index <- (index - 1) %/% 26
  }
  paste0("T", paste0(label, collapse = ""))
}
word_table <- function(data, caption, notes, digits = 3, headers = names(data),
                       groups = NULL) {
  group_rows <- integer()
  if (!is.null(groups)) {
    if (is.null(names(groups)) || anyNA(groups) || any(groups < 1L) ||
        any(groups != as.integer(groups)) || sum(groups) != nrow(data))
      stop("Invalid Word table groups: ", caption)
    blocks <- list()
    offset <- 0L
    for (i in seq_along(groups)) {
      heading <- as.data.frame(as.list(c(names(groups)[i], rep("", ncol(data) - 1L))),
                               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
      names(heading) <- names(data)
      rows <- seq.int(offset + 1L, offset + groups[i])
      blocks[[i]] <- rbind(heading, data[rows, , drop = FALSE])
      group_rows <- c(group_rows, offset + i)
      offset <- offset + groups[i]
    }
    data <- do.call(rbind, blocks)
  }
  table <- flextable::flextable(data)
  table <- flextable::set_header_labels(table, values = setNames(headers, names(data)))
  table <- flextable::colformat_int(table, big.mark = "", na_str = "")
  table <- flextable::colformat_double(table, digits = digits, big.mark = "", na_str = "")
  table <- flextable::theme_booktabs(table)
  table <- flextable::font(table, fontname = "Arial", part = "all")
  table <- flextable::fontsize(table, size = 9, part = "all")
  table <- flextable::padding(table, padding = 3, part = "all")
  table <- flextable::align(table, align = "left", part = "all")
  if (ncol(data) > 1L)
    table <- flextable::align(table, j = 2:ncol(data), align = "right", part = "body")
  for (row in group_rows) {
    table <- flextable::merge_at(table, i = row, j = seq_len(ncol(data)), part = "body")
    table <- flextable::italic(table, i = row, italic = TRUE, part = "body")
    table <- flextable::align(table, i = row, align = "left", part = "body")
  }
  table <- flextable::autofit(table)
  table <- flextable::fit_to_width(table, max_width = 6.5)
  table <- flextable::set_table_properties(
    table, layout = "fixed", align = "left",
    opts_word = list(split = FALSE, repeat_headers = TRUE)
  )
  table <- flextable::paginate(table, init = FALSE, hdr_ftr = TRUE)
  cat("\n\n", caption, "\n\n")
  flextable::flextable_to_rmd(table)
  cat("\n\n", notes, "\n\n")
}
technical_table_number <- 0L
report_table <- function(x, name, digits = 3, page_by = NULL) {
  spec <- table_specs[[name]]
  if (is.null(spec)) stop("Missing table specification: ", name)
  tables <- if (is.null(page_by)) list(x) else
    split(x, factor(x[[page_by]], levels = unique(x[[page_by]])))
  markdown <- character()
  for (table in tables) {
    title <- spec$title
    if (!is.null(page_by)) {
      key <- unique(table[[page_by]])
      if (length(key) != 1L || !key %in% names(outcome_labels))
        stop("Missing outcome label for table: ", name)
      title <- paste(title, outcome_labels[[key]], sep = ": ")
      table[[page_by]] <- NULL
      if ("weighting" %in% names(table) && !"weighting" %in% names(spec$columns)) {
        if (length(unique(table$weighting)) != 1L)
          stop("Mixed weighting schemes in table: ", name)
        table$weighting <- NULL
      }
    }
    if (!setequal(names(table), names(spec$columns)))
      stop("Column definitions do not match displayed columns in table: ", name)
    if (!is.null(spec$headers) && !setequal(names(table), names(spec$headers)))
      stop("Column headers do not match displayed columns in table: ", name)
    headers <- if (is.null(spec$headers)) names(table) else unname(spec$headers[names(table)])
    technical_table_number <<- technical_table_number + 1L
    caption <- sprintf("Table %s. %s", technical_table_id(technical_table_number), title)
    notes <- paste(
      "NOTES.",
      paste(paste0(headers, ": ", spec$columns[names(table)]), collapse = " "),
      spec$note
    )
    markdown <- c(markdown, caption, "",
                  as.character(knitr::kable(table, format = "pipe", digits = digits,
                                           row.names = FALSE, col.names = headers)), "", notes, "")
    if (!is.null(page_by)) cat("\n\n::: {.page}\n::: {.small}\n\n")
    word_table(table, caption, notes, digits = digits, headers = headers)
    if (!is.null(page_by)) cat("\n\n:::\n:::\n\n")
  }
  writeLines(markdown, here::here("MD", paste0(analysis, "_", name, ".md")))
}
format_estimate <- function(key, metric = "Kappa") {
  a <- agreement[agreement$outcome_stage == key & agreement$group == "Overall" &
                   agreement$weighting == primary_weighting & agreement$metric == metric, ]
  if (nrow(a) != 1L) stop("Expected one primary manuscript estimate: ", key, "; ", metric)
  if (!is.finite(a$estimate)) return("undefined because the category margins yield no estimable coefficient")
  if (!is.finite(a$lower)) return(sprintf("%.3f (95%% CI unavailable; inspect bootstrap diagnostics)", a$estimate))
  sprintf("%.3f (95%% CI %.3f to %.3f)", a$estimate, a$lower, a$upper)
}

::: {.page}

## Purpose and design

This is a re-analysis of agreement of delirium severity among 7 BASIL reference standard clinical raters as described in the draft manuscript **_Inter-rater reliability of delirium severity ratings using a standardized clinical assessment of delirium in at-risk patients_** (AMGP-26-510). The main analytic criticism was lack of clarity among statistical methods and failure to use standard methods for multiple rater reliability assessment, and reporting Pearson's correlations when kappa statistics are more standard. The new analysis extends Conger's kappa to incorporate entropy-balanced participant weights. These estimates are the primary results. We retain the all-pairs data structure only for preparing graphical displays of agreement. We no longer report correlation coefficients, only kappas and absolute deviations (differences).

Conger's kappa is a chance-corrected agreement statistic that accommodates category weights (providing partial credit for close severity ratings). Category weights and participant weights serve different purposes. The primary analysis uses entropy balancing to match the reliability sample to the full BASIL cohort on mean reference-standard delirium severity and site proportions. Equal-participant-weight results are retained only in the technical report for comparison and implementation validation. Conger's kappa and pooled all-pairs Cohen's kappa may be numerically similar, but they are not algebraically equivalent.

A potential point of confusion is that weights enter the reliability assessment in the agreement cells. Weights also enter the analysis at the individual participant level to account for differences in the sampled persons from the overall basal sample. This has to be described carefully.

This analysis report does four main things:

1. We describe the new analyses in technical and computational detail, and high-level statistical results that are not ready for manuscript presentation.
2. We describe the statistical results.
3. We identify text in the submitted manuscript, reprint it as struck out text, and replace it with new text that reflects the new analyses.
4. We present a new set of tables and figures to replace the original tables and figures in the submitted manuscript.

Technical tables are labelled Table TA, Table TB, and so on: "T" denotes "Technical output," and the letters index tables in report order. After Table TZ, the sequence continues with Table TAA, Table TAB, and so on. Tables prepared for the revised manuscript retain their manuscript labels (Table 1, Supplemental Table 1, and Supplemental Table 2), so they can be distinguished from the technical output.

References to original manuscript passages use page numbers in the current PDF, counting from its title page as page 1. These refer to pages in the source manuscript, not pages in this analysis report.

This analysis report is not a point-by-point response of reviewer critiques, and it is not a comprehensive revision of the submitted manuscript. Nevertheless, it is informative of those end products. In this report, we refer to "analysis1" that is the analysis done for the submitted manuscript. This analysis is referred to as "analysis2."

:::

::: {.page}

## Inputs and missing ratings

The import and participant-level harmonization were adapted from Analysis1's 030, 040, and 045 scripts. The local workbook is `SourceData/FINAL RS IRR Ratings.xlsx`; the parent-cohort inputs are `BASILIIMainStudy_Derived.dta` and `n488.dta` in the relative folder specified in this control file. As in Analysis1, Tamara's rows are excluded, participant identifiers are trimmed before joining, and a rating without an arrow is carried forward as its post-discussion rating. Those carried-forward ratings do not establish that a case was discussed.

Available ratings are used without imputing absent reviewer scores. Each outcome is checked separately. Participants with fewer than 2 ratings or a reviewer with no ratings cause the run to stop. A complete-participant sensitivity estimate drops participants missing any of the 7 ratings for that outcome and stage.

## Agreement and uncertainty

The primary estimate is calculated with our participant-weighted extension of Conger's kappa. We adapted the [irrCAC implementation](https://github.com/cran/irrCAC/blob/master/R/agree.coeff3.raw.r) so that entropy-balanced participant weights enter both observed agreement and each reviewer's category proportions. This is our extension, rather than a participant-weighting option in the package. With every participant weight set to 1, our code is checked against `irrCAC::conger.kappa.raw` for each estimable outcome, stage, and dementia group; the technical tables report the differences, and the run stops if any exceed 0.00001. Installed irrCAC version: `r as.character(packageVersion("irrCAC"))`; R version: `r as.character(getRversion())`.

Cohen's kappa summarizes agreement between 2 reviewers, whereas Conger's kappa extends the calculation to a panel of reviewers. Both compare observed agreement ($P_o$) with the agreement expected from reviewers' separate use of the rating categories ($P_e$):

$$
\kappa = \frac{P_o-P_e}{1-P_e}.
$$

A value of 1 indicates perfect agreement; 0 indicates agreement equal to that expected under this chance model; negative values indicate less agreement than expected. This chance model assumes independent ratings with each reviewer's observed category proportions.

For Cohen's kappa, expected agreement is calculated from the category proportions of the 2 reviewers:

$$
P_e^{\mathrm{Cohen}} = \sum_a \sum_b w_{ab}\,p_{1a}\,p_{2b}.
$$

Here, $p_{ja}$ is the proportion of reviewer $j$'s available ratings in category $a$, and $w_{ab}$ is the agreement credit for ratings $a$ and $b$. Traditional, unweighted Cohen's kappa gives credit only to identical ratings ($w_{ab}=1$ if $a=b$, and 0 otherwise). Weighted kappa also gives partial credit to close ratings.

Conger's kappa averages expected agreement across all distinct reviewer pairs, retaining each reviewer's own category proportions. For our 7 reviewers, there are 21 pairs:

$$
P_e^{\mathrm{Conger}} =
\frac{1}{21}\sum_{j<k}\sum_a\sum_b w_{ab}\,p_{ja}\,p_{kb}.
$$

For standard Conger's kappa, observed agreement is calculated by averaging agreement credit across available reviewer pairs within each participant, then across participants. Conger's kappa combines observed and expected agreement into a single panel estimate, rather than averaging 21 separately calculated kappas. With only 2 reviewers, it reduces to Cohen's kappa using the same agreement weights. For severity scores on our 0-10 scale, $w_{ab}=1-(a-b)^2/100$; for delirium presence, only identical ratings receive credit.

:::

::: {.page}

### Participant-weighted extension

Our extension retains the same kappa formula and distinct-reviewer-pair calculation of expected agreement. We replace equal-participant averages with entropy-weighted averages. If $v_i$ is participant $i$'s entropy weight, $R_{ij}$ is reviewer $j$'s rating, and $A_i$ is the average agreement credit across available reviewer pairs for that participant, then

$$
P_o = \frac{\sum_i v_i A_i}{\sum_i v_i},
\qquad
p_{ja} =
\frac{\sum_{i:\,R_{ij}\ \mathrm{observed}} v_i\,\mathbf{1}(R_{ij}=a)}
{\sum_{i:\,R_{ij}\ \mathrm{observed}} v_i}.
$$

The indicator $\mathbf{1}(R_{ij}=a)$ is 1 when the rating equals category $a$ and 0 otherwise. These weighted category proportions are substituted into $P_e^{\mathrm{Conger}}$. Setting every $v_i=1$ recovers the standard equal-participant-weight calculation. The primary estimates use the entropy weights; the equal-weight special case is used for validation and technical comparison.

Uncertainty is summarized by percentile 95% confidence intervals from `r B` bootstrap samples of participants. All reviewer columns and the observed missingness pattern travel together. The same participant sample is used for initial and post-discussion κ when estimating their paired change. Reviewers are treated as a fixed panel, so these intervals describe uncertainty across participants conditional on the 7 reviewers; they do not quantify variation over a population of reviewers.
:::

Severity exact agreement, agreement within 2 points, and mean absolute difference (MAD) are calculated from category counts within each participant, then averaged using the entropy-balanced participant weights. A participant's overall contribution depends on the entropy weight, rather than the number of available reviewer pairs. This calculation preserves the original within-2-point definition without using a pooled all-pairs dataset for statistics. Binary exact agreement is summarized in the same manner. Proportions are shown on a 0–1 scale.

Agreement is estimated separately for participants with and without reference-standard dementia. These estimates describe agreement within each group. Comparisons of kappa require caution because the distribution of rating categories influences the coefficient; differences do not by themselves establish differences in reviewer performance, and similar estimates do not establish equivalent agreement. The paired change describes the difference between stages; without a control group it cannot identify the causal effect of discussion.

:::

::: {.page}

## Participant weighting

The primary analysis uses entropy balancing to match the reliability sample to the full enrolled cohort on mean reference-standard delirium severity and the proportions of participants included at sites 2 and 3. These weights balance the specified covariate means; extending agreement estimates to the full cohort still requires assumptions about rating behavior beyond the selected sample.

**_Difference from Analysis1:_** Analysis2 uses the full enrolled cohort of 488 participants as the entropy-balancing target, consistent with the manuscript's stated aim of matching the reliability sample to the full BASIL II sample. Analysis1's code instead matched the 46 reliability participants to the 442 participants outside that sample. This change aligns the weighting target with the stated aim; it is separate from the change to Conger's kappa. Weighting balances mean reference-standard delirium severity and site proportions, but does not establish that agreement in the selected reliability sample generalizes to the full cohort.

:::

The `weights` argument of `conger.kappa.raw` specifies category agreement weights, not participant sampling weights. Our primary procedure is a participant-weighted extension of that implementation. Participant weights enter both observed agreement and each reviewer's category margins. They are held fixed within bootstrap samples; those intervals condition on the estimated weights and target moments and omit weight-estimation uncertainty. The full-cohort interpretation requires that the selected cases adequately represent rating behavior after balancing the measured covariates. Balancing cannot establish that assumption.

The effective sample size (ESS) is the squared sum of participant weights divided by their sum of squares. Its relation to the number of reliability participants helps identify concentration of weights. Weighted subgroup estimates inherit the overall weights; no separate dementia target is imposed.

:::

::: {.page}

## Descriptive pooled reviewer-pair displays

The displays include all observed unique reviewer pairs within each participant. The first and second reviewer refer to the lower and higher fixed reviewer-column indices, respectively; they do not identify 2 particular reviewers. Each participant contributes multiple dependent points. Point sizes show raw comparison counts. These graphics use no participant weights and contain no pooled κ, correlation, regression test, or confidence interval.

## Differences across severity levels

```{r}
#| label: initial-difference
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-alt: "Initial signed reviewer differences plotted against their mean severity, with reference lines at zero and plus or minus two."
knitr::include_graphics(plot_paths[["initial_difference"]])
```

```{r}
#| label: consensus-difference
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-alt: "Post-discussion signed reviewer differences plotted against their mean severity, with reference lines at zero and plus or minus two."
knitr::include_graphics(plot_paths[["consensus_difference"]])
```

These Bland–Altman-style displays show signed differences. Positive and negative differences may cancel, and reversing the reviewer order reverses their sign. A flat signed trend would therefore not establish constant absolute disagreement across severity. Reference lines at ±2 mark the prespecified tolerance, not estimated limits of agreement. No conventional independent-pair limits of agreement or slope tests are computed for these dependent pooled comparisons.

:::

## Items requiring author input

The reviewer-response outline leaves the rating rubric, rationale for the severity measure, possible CAM-S comparison, and several clinical design questions unresolved (Internal: REFERENCES/AMGP-26-510-reviews-RESPONSES.md, Reviewer 2, comments 2–4; Reviewer 3; Reviewer 4). The analysis implements the specified agreement revision. It does not invent rating anchors, equate packet-rating agreement with instrument validity, or add diagnostic sensitivity and specificity without an agreed reference-standard comparison plan. The manuscript describes broad severity anchors on PDF p. 7; a complete rubric and its instructions still require author confirmation.

The retained participant data include reference-standard dementia severity and CAM-S for later author-directed descriptive work. Initial and post-discussion score distributions, missingness, and dementia composition should be checked against the manuscript before submission. Existing numerical claims are replaced only when this report is executed locally.
